title: Your B12 Isn't From a Cow—It's a Microbial Masterpiece
summary: Vitamin B12, vital for human health, is uniquely synthesized by bacteria and archaea, not by plants, animals, or fungi. The human liver remarkably stores a three-year supply, which often masks deficiencies for extended periods.
content:
Picture your bloodstream, a bustling highway of nutrients. Among them, cruising along, are vital molecules of vitamin B12, tirelessly working to support everything from nerve function to red blood cell production. Here’s the mind-bending truth, often overlooked even by health enthusiasts: every single one of these B12 molecules was, at some point in its long history, forged by a microbe.

Forget the common misconception that B12 comes directly from meat or plants. Neither cows nor spinach leaves, nor any animal, plant, or fungus on Earth, possess the intricate biological machinery to produce this essential compound. Instead, this crucial vitamin is the exclusive handiwork of microscopic bacteria and archaea, ancient life forms that have quietly underpinned our planet's biochemistry for eons. It’s a profound reminder of our deep, symbiotic reliance on the microbial world.

Humans, along with other animals, acquire B12 indirectly, primarily by consuming animal products where these hardworking microbes have done their work, or through increasingly common fortified foods. What's truly astonishing, however, is our body's exceptional storage capacity for this microbially-gifted nutrient. Your liver acts as a sophisticated biological vault, capable of hoarding enough B12 to sustain you for roughly three years.

This remarkable, long-term reserve is both a blessing and a challenge. While it provides a substantial buffer against immediate scarcity, ensuring consistent supply for vital processes, it also means that the signs of deficiency can remain insidiously hidden for an extended period – sometimes years – before manifesting in blood tests or noticeable symptoms affecting the nervous system or red blood cell formation. This delay underscores the silent, yet foundational, role microbes play in our fundamental health, orchestrating an unseen supply chain crucial for our well-being.
keyTakeaways: Vitamin B12 is exclusively synthesized by bacteria and archaea; no plants, animals, or fungi can produce it.
Humans obtain B12 indirectly, primarily through animal products or fortified foods, highlighting our reliance on microbial processes.
The human liver can store approximately a three-year supply of B12, which can significantly delay the detection of deficiency.
author: Space Daily Editorial Team

title: The Ghost Fleet of Roswell: Where Classic Cars Met Cosmic Secrets
summary: Roswell's legendary A-1 Auto Salvage, once a treasure trove of over 500 classic vehicles, offered a unique blend of automotive history and extraterrestrial mystique. Its unexpected closure left behind unanswered questions, fueling local legends about what cosmic secrets might have been buried beneath its rusting metal.
content:
For dedicated automotive archaeologists, A-1 Auto Salvage in Roswell, New Mexico, wasn't just a junkyard; it was a sprawling, sun-baked museum of forgotten Americana. With well over 500 classic cars and trucks scattered across its dusty expanse, it was a veritable paradise for those seeking a glimpse into the past, a treasure chest of steel and chrome waiting to be unearthed. Each rust-eaten fender and shattered windshield held stories, silently bearing witness to decades of desert life.

But this wasn't just any salvage yard. This was Roswell. In a town synonymous with the otherworldly, where the very air seems to hum with unexplained phenomena, even a collection of vintage vehicles takes on an entirely different aura. One couldn't help but wonder what these metallic sentinels had *seen*. Did a '57 Chevy pickup, abandoned to the elements, once cruise past a hushed military convoy in the dead of night? Did the bent chassis of an old Ford ever feel the vibrations of something truly alien landing just beyond the horizon?

Sadly, the chance to ponder these cosmic-automotive connections is gone forever. Within a few short years of its golden age, A-1 Auto Salvage closed its gates for good, its vast inventory dispersed or crushed into oblivion. The closure wasn't just the end of a business; it was the disappearance of a unique cultural artifact, a tangible link to both the golden age of American motoring and the enduring, whispered legends of Roswell. What secrets, if any, were hauled away with the final load of scrap metal?

Today, the site is quiet, devoid of the echoing calls of curious explorers or the metallic groans of shifting wrecks. But the legend of A-1 Auto Salvage, and the cosmic questions it inadvertently raised, continues to linger, an indelible part of Roswell's peculiar tapestry.
keyTakeaways: A-1 Auto Salvage in Roswell, New Mexico, was a unique and extensive collection of over 500 classic vehicles.
Its location in Roswell infused the car yard with an additional layer of mystery, connecting automotive history with local extraterrestrial lore.
The unexpected closure of A-1 Auto Salvage meant the loss of a significant historical and potentially legendary site for both automotive enthusiasts and UFO mystery buffs.
author: Will Shiers

title: Humanity's Next Lunar Leap: Artemis II Crew Thanks European Service Module Architects
summary: The four Artemis II astronauts recently visited ESA's technical site in the Netherlands, extending heartfelt gratitude to the dedicated team behind the European Service Module. This crucial module will power their Orion spacecraft on an upcoming human mission around the Moon, underscoring the vital international collaboration driving humanity's return to lunar exploration.
content:
The four astronauts poised to make humanity's next significant leap around the Moon, the crew of Artemis II, recently embarked on a crucial terrestrial mission: a heartfelt thank you tour. Their latest stop brought them to ESA’s sprawling technical site in Noordwijk, the Netherlands, where they met the unsung heroes responsible for the very heart of their Orion spacecraft – the European Service Module (ESM). It was a moment of profound connection between those who will fly to the stars and those who engineer their way there.

Commander Reid Wiseman, Pilot Victor Glover, Mission Specialist Christina Koch, and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen stood face-to-face with the brilliant minds who designed, built, and tested the ESM. This sophisticated powerhouse isn't merely a propulsion unit; it’s the lifeblood of Orion, providing essential functions like propulsion, power, thermal control, and the vital consumables – water and oxygen – that will sustain them far beyond Earth orbit. For a mission designed to carry humans further than ever before since Apollo, the ESM represents an indispensable European contribution to NASA’s ambitious lunar program.

The visit transcended a mere technical briefing. It was a powerful acknowledgment of the intricate, international collaboration propelling humanity back to the Moon. The astronauts expressed their immense confidence and gratitude, recognizing the countless hours of dedication poured into ensuring their safety and mission success. For the ESA engineers and technicians, many of whom have devoted years to this complex module, it was an incredibly proud moment to see the faces of those who will trust their lives to their craftsmanship.

As Artemis II prepares to make history, orbiting the Moon and paving the way for future lunar landings, the synergy between NASA and ESA shines brighter than ever. This pivotal module, assembled and tested in Bremen, Germany, under Airbus Defense and Space's prime contract, symbolizes Europe's integral role in the future of deep space exploration. The encounter in the Netherlands wasn't just a meeting; it was a testament to shared dreams and the collective human spirit pushing the boundaries of what's possible, one meticulously engineered component at a time.
keyTakeaways: The Artemis II astronaut crew visited ESA's technical site in the Netherlands to personally thank the team behind the European Service Module (ESM).
The ESM is a vital component of the Orion spacecraft, providing critical propulsion, power, and life support systems for the upcoming human mission around the Moon.
This visit underscored the profound international collaboration between NASA and ESA, highlighting Europe's essential contribution to humanity's return to lunar exploration.
author: Staff Writer
